To a crown's crew he is the prize every ministry in Europe would most like to bring home.
Hooks

items: A letter in the great artificer's hand reaches a party member abroad, answering a question they asked a Mutapan lamp-tuner in passing a year ago. It invites them to Sofala. The guild has a copy.
His construct has walked out of the workshop at night and is standing at the guild hall's door. Nobody sent it, and it won't move.
The Shava house's men came back, and this time they took his notebook from the 1630s. He wants it back before the court learns it was ever gone.
He wants passage on the party's ship, under another name, as far as Surat. He won't say where he goes after that.

blocks.text: Shiri

A Counsellor (Spymaster), about forty-five, and Mutapa's foreign intelligence. Her agents call her Shiri, "bird" in Shona, after the soapstone bird on her seal, and she has never corrected them. Her own name is in the ledgers of the House of the Bird, Mutapa's bank, and nowhere else.

She grew up at the fair at Dambarare, where foreign traders live and trade on the king's leave, the daughter of one of the king's customs officers. By twelve she spoke Shona, Swahili, Portuguese and enough Gujarati to know what a trader said when he thought no one at the scales could follow. The House of the Bird took her on as a clerk of correspondents' letters. She noticed that a bill of exchange says who trusts whom, and that the Bird's correspondents, read together, say what every court is about to do: who is borrowing for a fleet, who has stopped paying, who is buying platinum and at what price. She asked to read them on purpose. The Bird made her its reader, and when the court began selling abroad, its reader became its spymaster.

She runs the thinnest service in the world from one room above the bank, with one window, a table and a bench. Her assets are a handful of factors in the ports, the Bird's correspondents, and a few Mhizha abroad who retune curiosities in great houses and write home about what they see (Characters, Mutapan Agent). She has never met most of them. Every report is answered by the next ship, even if the answer is one line, and every agent is paid on time, every time.

She belongs to the Spymaster's Club, as every court's spymaster does, and she is the only member whose king makes the stones. She buys introductions and the use of the Club's stones from its London chair like everyone else. The others assume she can hear through the shewstones; she lets them assume it, and nobody knows whether she can.

In 1668 she is watching four things: the London artificer and his English apprentice; who told Spain what its platina was; the shewstone push, which she and the great artificer are the two to see clearly; and above all the gate at Toledo and the warded blank, which she means to understand before Europe acts. She and Simbarashe Moyo agree about the stones and about little else. His choice is the thing she most fears and can least prevent, and she has a file on him as thick as any court's.

**At the table.** A party meets her factor first, and gets its orders by letter under the bird seal. A crew that does three jobs well is asked up the stairs, once, to the bench in the room above the bank. As a patron she pays in gold by the *mithqal* and in credit on the Bird, and she never asks a party to do what it can't. As an opponent she seldom kills. She ruins credit: a factor stops honoring your paper, a harbor master finds your papers wanting, and a European crew discovers that nobody in any port will lend to it. As a mirror for a party's own spymaster, she is what the job looks like with a tenth of the money. On the fair's rest day she plays tsoro in the market at Sofala with whoever sits down, and loses on purpose to children.
Hooks

items: Her factor in Venice has stopped answering. She wants to know whether he is dead, turned or in love, and she wants the answer before the Sensa.
A Mutapan factor in Lisbon has been seen going in at the Holy Office's side door. She wants him followed for a week, and stopped only if he goes in a second time.
One of her Mhizha abroad has started writing home in a cipher she never gave him.
She wants to know who is paying for the great artificer's passage. She doesn't say what she will do with the answer.

blocks.text: Simon Horowitz
A Warlock (Envoy), about thirty-five, and the Kabbalist of Venice's ghetto. He is the Venice Job's contact.

He is a Horowitz of Prague, of the Levite family that built a synagogue there, and his grandfather brought the household to Venice. He belongs to the ghetto's German congregation and lives on the fourth floor above a synagogue door. He earns his living by reading: contracts, old deeds and, for the Council of Ten, any hand their own clerks can't make out. The Republic locks the ghetto's gates at sunset and opens them at dawn, so he works at night, at a borrowed table, by a candle-end.

Two years ago much of the ghetto believed Sabbatai Zevi was the messiah, and some families sold their leases and furniture to be ready. Then Sabbatai Zevi took the turban before the sultan. Simon hadn't believed, and being right didn't make him kinder: he trusts no one who promises anything. In March 1668 the messiah's prophet, Nathan of Gaza, lands at Venice, and the rabbis and the city make him sign that his prophecies were his own imagination. Simon is asked to read the hand of the confession.

**The book.** An angel gave Simon a book and told him to read it. By default the angel is Raziel, the keeper of secrets, who in Kabbalist tradition gave a book to the first man; that is why the gift came as a book. Simon can read the script and can't yet read the language. Each page gives way after weeks of work, and each page he reads is something he can then do, which is how he comes by an Envoy's powers (*The Classes*, Warlock, Envoy). He is eleven pages in. What the book is for belongs to the table; by default it is the book Raziel gave the first man, and its last page opens a door the angel wants opened.

**The golem.** The ghetto's golem was made in Prague in the 1580s, in Rabbi Loew's time. Nobody in Venice knows why it walked there. By default it followed the word: Simon's grandfather knew the word that stops it, and when he moved his household to Venice the golem came after. The burial society knows the word now, and so does Simon. The golem guards the ghetto after dark, never strikes first and lets pass anyone who tells it the truth about why they have come (Adventures and Hooks, The Venice Job).

**At the table.** Simon is young, sleepless and sharp-tongued. He is a contact first: he reads what nobody else can, he knows how the Ten lock their rooms and he can walk a party past the golem. As a teacher he takes an Envoy or a Wizard who will work, and he asks to be paid in texts: a copied page, a borrowed manuscript, a letter carried to Prague or Amsterdam and the answer brought back. As a patron he hires for whatever he can't do from behind locked gates. A party that says plainly what it wants from him, and what it will take, gets further than one that flatters or promises.
Hooks

items: The twelfth page names a house in Venice outside the ghetto, and Simon can't go there after dark. He wants someone to go, and to tell him exactly what is over the door.
The Ten send him a letter to read. It is in his own hand, and he never wrote it.
The golem has started stopping at Simon's door each night and waiting. It last did that the week his grandfather died.

Nathan of Gaza is being sent on to Livorno under escort. One family in the ghetto wants him to slip the escort, the rabbis want him delivered, and Simon wants ten minutes with him first, to ask what he saw.

blocks.text: The Sharper and the Wit

Two more: a Gamester and a Courtier, a couple who work as a pair, written as player characters a table can take as they are, or meet as rivals across a gaming table. They're English, in their twenties, and banned from more houses than most people have visited. Louche, loud, very funny about the English, and much better brought up than they let on.

**Kit Harrow**, Counsellor (Gamester), 24. A Cavalier baronet's daughter. Her father came home with the king in 1660 and lost the estate at hazard at the Groom Porter's inside two years. Kit learned the game to win it back, and found she was better at it than anyone she'd ever met. She never stopped. She plays in breeches because skirts catch on the table, and because the playhouses have made breeches on a woman the fashion. She does the season like a campaign: Whitehall in the winter, Tunbridge Wells for the waters and the card rooms in summer, Paris when London gets too hot, and the bear garden at Bankside when she's bored, in a borrowed coat and a borrowed accent. She keeps a pocketbook of every debt anyone owes her, including the ones she's forgiven, and she's never once been seen to count. She is owed money by two earls and a bishop. She owes it to one moneylender in Lombard Street, who is very patient, and very frightening.

**Ned Ashcombe**, Courtier (College of Verse), 26. The younger son of a Royalist colonel killed at Worcester, raised on a promise the Restoration hasn't kept. He came to Whitehall with nothing but a good leg, a better ear and a talent for lampoons. His lampoons are portraits of types: the clerk who keeps his wife's miniature in his desk and his mistress's in his hat, the country squire up for the season who bets the harvest on a cockfight, the courtier so fashionable he's out of date by Tuesday. Everyone in London can sing them, and everyone is sure the next verse is about the man beside them. One got him banished from the court for a season; he spent it in Paris and came back with better French and worse habits. He fences well and insists he doesn't, which the men he lampoons find out when they come looking for him. He has fought five duels and lost none, mostly because he made his opponents laugh.

**The couple.** They met across a hazard table at the Groom Porter's, where Ned tried to cheat her and Kit let him, to see how good he was. They were married a year later in the Fleet, by a parson who asked no questions, on a bet Kit won. Ned maintains it doesn't count and has never once tried to prove it. They fight in public, in verse and in arithmetic, and the town takes sides; nobody has ever seen either of them take a side against the other.

**The act.** The Gamester never leaves her chair; the Wit never seems to be at the table at all. Kit plays, and Ned works the room: who's drunk, who's desperate, who has a wife who'd like to know where her pearls went. A couplet in his mouth is a signal to her (a rhyme on the king means the bank is weak; a line of Donne means the man on her left is cheating), and nobody in Europe listens to Ned closely enough to notice. When the house turns ugly, she counts and he ripostes, and they leave by the window. Neither of them has ever left a gaming house by the front door twice. They end most nights at dawn in St James's Park, among the king's new ducks and the clerks walking to work, with somebody else's money and nowhere in particular to be.

**Where they're banned.** The Groom Porter's, for a season; the Duke of York's apartments, for a lampoon; two *académies de jeu* in Paris, for winning; a Rhenish bishop's palace, for reasons both tell differently. Venice's Ridotto still lets them in, wearing masks like everyone else, which suits them both.
**At the table.**

items: *As player characters,* both are 8th level, and their sheets are published separately. They're the pair for an intrigue game: Kit's Everyone's a Mark finds the tell, and Ned's Read finds who holds the power. In a fight, Kit's Big Player puts Ned where he needs to be, and her Know the Odds tells him exactly how much is left to cut.

*As NPCs,* they're the party's best friends or its worst rivals at any table in Europe (cross one of them and you've crossed both), and the people every Spymaster's Club agent would like to recruit, since no one notices who they talk to.
*As a team,* every debt is a hook. Somebody owes them; somebody they owe is losing patience.

blocks.text: Hooks

items: Kit has won a sealed dispatch case at ombre from a drunk envoy, and has no idea what is in it. Someone does, and is already at her lodging.
Ned's latest lampoon names no one, and everyone at court thinks it's about them. A duke wants the author's name; the author wants the party to find out which duke.
The patient moneylender in Lombard Street has finally called Kit's debt, and he doesn't want money. He wants her to lose one game, on purpose, at the Ridotto, to a man who has never lost.

A rival offers Ned a place at court, a pension and a wife with an estate, if he'll swear the Fleet marriage was a joke. He's asked the party to find out who's paying for the offer, and he hasn't told Kit.

blocks.text: Gottlieb von Schleich

A Counsellor (Spymaster) and Wizard, about fifty, and the man nobody invites. He's a Freiherr from a corner of Franconia, and envoy to the Perpetual Diet at Regensburg for an imperial county so small that it shares one vote with a whole bench of counts. The Diet opened in 1663 and never closed, so Schleich has had five years with nothing to do, and he has filled them by going everywhere.

He is at every reception in Regensburg and Vienna, every wedding, every lying-in-state, every opera and every hunt, at the edge of every conversation that matters, holding a glass he never drinks. Three courts have licensed him as a wizard, because none of them could find a reason not to. He's damp, attentive and agreeable; he laughs a moment after everyone else; he remembers your mother's name and your debts. He writes it all down in a small green book. He is never quite rude enough to be shown the door, and he always knows which door you came in by.

**At the table.** The party meets him in every city, and he has always heard. He offers help nobody asked for, and it's always good. The table's slow discovery is that he is never wrong, and that somebody is paying for the green book: his county can't afford his coat.
Hooks

items: Schleich greets the party by name in a city they arrived in that morning, and congratulates them on a job they haven't taken yet.
The green book has been stolen. Half of Vienna is relieved; the other half has started to worry about who has it now. Schleich asks the party to get it back, and to not read it.
Someone has finally poisoned Schleich, not fatally, and he wants to know who. He has a list, and it's long.
A minister offers the party a fortune to find out who Schleich reports to. The first clue is a bill for the coat.
